title: Representation Learning via Composite Subspace Flow Matching

paper.title: Representation Learning via Composite Subspace Flow Matching
paper.abstract:
Abstract Distilling semantic meaning from raw image data remains a challenge in machine learning.
Current self-supervised paradigms face a trade-off: joint-embedding architectures produce relevant features by aggressively discarding intra-class variance, irreversibly spatial and reconstruction.
Conversely, generative models preserve spatial details but struggle to isolate semantics, as their optimization is dominated by pixel variations.
To bridge this divide, we propose composite subspace flow matching (CSFM).
Rather than corrupting data with unstructured isotropic noise, CSFM formulates representation learning as the variance-minimizing inversion of a deterministic degradation curriculum across spectral, color, and illumination subspaces.
By bounding trajectory variance with hard temporal style truncation, a capacity-constrained encoder is driven to ignore transient style artifacts and encode persistent content.
Empirical evaluations across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10 show that CSFM yields competitive discriminative transferability while preserving generative synthesis across both convolutional and vision transformer architectures.
By avoiding the collapse pathologies of non-generative methods, CSFM forms a smooth latent space that outperforms standard optimal transport flows on linear probing and few-shot classification, while enabling coherent synthesis and trajectory interpolation.
These results confirm that steering the physical dynamics of generative flows offers a scalable paradigm for learning representations that are simultaneously linearly separable and generatively invertible.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The primary objective of self-supervised representation learning is to extract informative, high-level, and useful features for downstream tasks from unlabeled raw data [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . While self-supervised learning (SSL) has catalyzed advances across computer vision, natural language processing, and world models for autonomous decision-making [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , extracting representations from unlabelled visual data remains challenging due to the high noise-to-signal ratio inherent to pixel space [ 8 ] . Unlike discrete textual tokens, which represent semantically compressed units, raw pixels are uncompressed physical measurements [ 8 ] . Consequently, high-magnitude nuisance variables, such as localized textures, illumination shifts, and background clutter, statistically dominate the input variance, frequently overshadowing the underlying semantic targets [ 9 , 10 ] . To address these nuisance factors, visual SSL research has largely split into two paradigms with conflicting trade-offs [ 8 ] . On the one hand, reconstruction-based architectures, such as masked autoencoders [ 11 ] and denoising autoencoders [ 12 , 13 ] , model the data distribution by inverting input-space corruptions. However, because standard L 2 L_{2} pixel recovery aligns with raw variance rather than semantic abstraction, these models remain biased toward unpredictable, high-variance details [ 14 , 7 , 10 ] . Conversely, joint-embedding architectures (JEAs), such as VICReg [ 15 ] , and LeJEPA [ 16 ] , circumvent pixel synthesis entirely by enforcing invariance across augmented views in a latent representation space [ 17 , 18 ] . Although this abstraction shields JEAs from nuisance variations, it leaves them vulnerable to informational and dimensional collapse [ 19 , 20 ] . More fundamentally, recent theoretical work reveals a structural friction between discriminative extraction and generative reversibility [ 21 , 8 , 10 ] . To maximize linear separability on semantic tasks, JEAs suppress all intra-class sensitivity. While this invariance maximizes classification margins, it permanently deletes high-frequency and spatial information, rendering the learned representations structurally irreversible and incapable of image synthesis [ 21 , 22 ] . Continuous-time generative models, specifically continuous normalizing flows and diffusion models [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] , provide fully invertible spatial transformations that preserve geometry [ 26 , 24 ] . Recognizing their capacity to model complex distributions without spatial loss, a recent paradigm shift repurposes continuous generative trajectories as proxy objectives for representation learning [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] . By conditioning a continuous vector field on a bottlenecked latent code, the encoder is driven to distill the sufficient statistics required to resolve trajectory ambiguities [ 29 , 30 ] . Because this objective relies on continuous trajectory reconstruction rather than explicit embedding-space invariance, it avoids the dimensional collapse common in JEAs while maintaining spatial reversibility [ 31 ] . Despite this promise, continuous representation models face a significant limitation: standard frameworks rely almost exclusively on isotropic Gaussian noise [ 25 , 23 , 32 ] . This spatially uncorrelated corruption perturbs all image coordinates independently and identically, without accounting for the underlying structure of visual data. Recent generative works have expanded beyond pure Gaussian noise by designing physical degradation trajectories, such as blurring or masking [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] . However, adapting these cumulative multi-operator processes to representation learning proves challenging: sequential noise injections incur an intractable covariance inversion cost and introduce an irreducible target noise floor that disrupts encoder optimization. To resolve these limitations while balancing representation quality with generative reversibility, we propose composite subspace flow matching (CSFM). It replaces uniform corruption with an ordered sequence of deterministic subspace projections spanning the frequency, color, and illumination domains. By pairing this composite drift with a single, decoupled isotropic noise schedule, CSFM yields a simulation-free target vector field that nullifies irreducible target noise with minimal computational overhead. Under this continuous curriculum, content is defined by temporal persistence under physical transport. CSFM isolates content within a capacity-bounded latent code while offloading transient spatial details to the generative vector field, balancing downstream linear separability with a smooth, reversible generative manifold. The core contributions of this work are three-fold: 1. Composite subspace flow matching (CSFM): we introduce a simulation-free flow matching framework that couples an ordered visual degradation path with a decoupled isotropic noise schedule, eliminating target velocity variance with minimal memory overhead 2. Optimal encoder geometry: we show that minimizing trajectory variance induces a block-diagonal precision geometry, prevents features from the style subspace from dominating encoder capacity, and proves that style truncation is necessary for content alignment. 3. Comprehensive empirical validation: across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10 ( 96 × 96 96\times 96 ), using CNN and vision transformer backbones, CSFM outperforms unguided flows and autoencoders in linear and few-shot probing while preserving an invertible, connected latent space for generative decoding. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews self-supervised representation learning paradigms, continuous normalizing flows, trajectory conditioning, and sketched Gaussian regularization. Section 3 introduces CSFM, including the composite projection curriculum, asymmetric gradient routing, and forward-mode analytical computation. Section 4 provides theoretical proofs for subspace disentanglement, capacity saturation, and the style truncation requirement. Section 5 presents empirical evaluations on representation quality, generative fidelity, and scalability across architectures and resolutions. Section 6 presents our conclusions and outlines directions for future work.

sections.heading: 2.1 Paradigms of Representation Learning: JEAs vs. Generative Models
sections.text: The goal of self-supervised representation learning is to extract from raw sensory data useful features for downstream tasks, while discarding task-irrelevant style and nuisance [ 36 , 15 , 16 ] . Following recent theoretical formulations [ 22 , 8 ] , an observation x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is decomposed into complementary orthogonal subspaces ℝ D = 𝒳 c ⊕ 𝒳 s \mathbb{R}^{D}=\mathcal{X}_{c}\oplus\mathcal{X}_{s} via x = x c + x s , x=x_{c}+x_{s}, (1) where content x c ∈ 𝒳 c x_{c}\in\mathcal{X}_{c} lies in a low-dimensional subspace ( dim ( 𝒳 c ) = c ≪ D \dim(\mathcal{X}_{c})=c\ll D ) and style x s ∈ 𝒳 s x_{s}\in\mathcal{X}_{s} occupies the orthogonal complement ( 𝒳 s = 𝒳 c ⟂ \mathcal{X}_{s}=\mathcal{X}_{c}^{\perp} ) [ 8 ] . Existing self-supervised methodologies target data decomposition through two diverging paradigms with contrasting trade-offs [ 8 ] . Reconstruction-based generative architectures, such as denoising autoencoders (DAE) [ 12 , 13 ] and masked autoencoders (MAE) [ 11 ] , learn by inverting input corruptions in pixel space [ 8 ] . While this ensures generative reversibility and preserves fine spatial, standard L 2 L_{2} pixel recovery optimizes for total raw variance rather than semantic features [ 14 , 7 ] . Consequently, the encoder exhausts substantial capacity fitting textures and high-variance background noise [ 8 ] . Conversely, JEAs bypass pixel synthesis entirely by training an encoder to match latent representations across independently augmented views [ 37 , 17 , 18 ] . Predicting strictly in latent space protects JEAs from raw pixel [ 8 ] . However, by aggressively discarding all variance orthogonal to the hand-crafted invariances, JEAs permanently discard spatial structure, yielding structurally irreversible representations that are insufficient for image reconstruction [ 21 , 22 ] .

sections.heading: Representational Collapse and Latent Regularization.
sections.text: A critical failure mode of optimizing latent invariance in JEAs without generative constraints is representational collapse, wherein representations degrade to a trivial constant vector (information collapse) or span a degenerate lower-dimensional subspace (dimensional collapse) [ 19 , 20 ] . While contrastive objectives [ 37 ] and covariance decorrelation penalties (e.g. VICReg [ 15 ] , Barlow Twins [ 19 ] ) prevent collapse, second-moment decorrelation incurs quadratic computational complexity and is insufficient to guarantee true Gaussianity, which is provably optimal for minimizing downstream prediction risk [ 16 ] . Leveraging the Cramér-Wold theorem, SIGReg matches random 1 1 D projections of the empirical characteristic function against an analytical standard normal with linear complexity, providing a robust, collapse-free bottleneck without variational sampling noise [ 16 ] .

sections.heading: The Irreducible Target Variance Floor.
sections.text: Under an L 2 L_{2} regression penalty, the optimal vector field converges to the conditional expectation v θ ∗ ​ ( x t , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ u t ∣ x t ] v_{\theta}^{*}(x_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}[u_{t}\mid x_{t}] [ 41 ] . (4) The loss is bounded below by the irreducible target variance arising from trajectory intersections where distinct conditional paths cross at identical space-time coordinates x t x_{t} [ 29 , 28 ] . Eliminating this residual target variance requires conditioning the flow field on a latent representation z z to disambiguate crossing trajectories, which forms the theoretical foundation for continuous flow-based representation learning [ 28 , 29 ] .

sections.heading: Structured Degradation vs. Decoupled Trajectories.
sections.text: Standard continuous generative models rely on isotropic Gaussian noise, which perturbs all pixel coordinates independently and identically, failing to capture the structured spatial, spectral, and photometric correlations of natural images [ 33 ] . While generalized diffusion models incorporate physical corruptions like blurring or heat dissipation [ 34 , 35 , 42 ] , they remain restricted to single diagonalizable operators to preserve analytical tractability. Extending this formulation to multiple operators reveals a computational divide: when the corruption operators commute, they admit a simultaneous eigenbasis, enabling closed-form conditioning and evaluation in 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}(D\log D) time. Conversely, composing non-commuting operators destroys this joint diagonalization, producing a dense marginal covariance whose inversion incurs an intractable 𝒪 ⁡ ( D 3 ) \mathcal{O}(D^{3}) computational cost. Regardless of commutativity, injecting independent noise across paths produces intersecting trajectories, creating an irreducible target variance floor that cannot be eliminated without latent conditioning. In parallel, masked modeling reveals that corrupting global spectral bases rather than localized spatial patches enhances semantic representation learning [ 43 ] . In a similar spirit of leveraging structured data transformations, CSFM embeds structured physical degradation into a continuous generative model: pairing a deterministic drift across canonical visual subspaces with a decoupled isotropic noise path steers the encoder toward persistent content at minimal computational cost.

sections.heading: Dynamics-Driven Persistence vs. Augmentation Invariance.
sections.text: This deterministic formulation shifts how content and style are separated. In joint-embedding architectures, content is defined by invariance to hand-crafted data augmentations (e.g. random crops and color jitter) [ 47 , 48 ] , discarding perturbed features as style and risking shortcut learning if heuristics misalign with underlying semantics [ 8 , 10 ] . In continuous flows, content is defined by temporal persistence under physical transport. Because transient fine-scale variations vanish early along the degradation trajectory, they induce large conditional velocity variance if predicted from degraded states. Consequently, the capacity-bounded encoder is driven to distill features that resolve global trajectory ambiguity, isolating content from continuous transport dynamics rather than synthetic view corruptions.

sections.heading: 4 Theoretical Analysis: Optimal Representation Geometry
sections.text: In this section, we characterize the optimal encoder geometry induced by the CSFM objective. We show that under finite capacity, minimizing trajectory variance forces the encoder into a block-diagonal precision geometry that concentrates representational precision within the content subspace.

sections.heading: Datasets and Evaluation Protocols.
sections.text: We validate our framework across three visual benchmarks [ 59 , 60 ] : CIFAR-10 ( 32 × 32 32\times 32 , 10 classes) for primary benchmarking and ablations; CIFAR-100 ( 32 × 32 32\times 32 , 100 classes) for granular category scaling; and STL-10 ( 96 × 96 96\times 96 ) for higher spatial resolution. For STL-10, unsupervised pre-training uses all 105k images (5k labeled + 100k unlabeled), while downstream probes evaluate on the standard 5k train and 8k test splits. Frozen representations are evaluated via linear probing, non-parametric k k -NN classification ( k = 20 k=20 ), and few-shot learning (1% and 10% labels per class) [ 37 , 11 ] . To measure latent cluster separation independently of classifiers, we report the silhouette score on test embeddings. Finally, secondary generative quality is evaluated in Appendix E via FID 1 ​ k \text{FID}_{1\text{k}} [ 61 ] , numerical ODE integration error, and latent space traversals.

sections.heading: Architectures and Capacity Scaling.
sections.text: To isolate decoupled transport dynamics from model size, backbones are benchmarked under multiple capacity controls: • Convolutional Models (NCSN++ U-Net): The representation encoder is a WideResNet-28-4 ( E ϕ E_{\phi} , 5.98M parameters, latent dimension c = 256 c=256 ) [ 62 ] . The vector field regressor ( v θ v_{\theta} ) is evaluated under three regimes: (i) Baseline (20.81M total): Base filters n ​ f = 64 nf=64 with channel multipliers ( 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 ) (1,2,2,2) and self-attention at 16 × 16 16\times 16 (14.83M U-Net parameters), serving as our primary ablation testbed. (ii) High-Capacity (65.08M total): Expanded filters n ​ f = 128 nf=128 with FIR anti-aliasing (59.10M U-Net parameters). Encoder capacity remains fixed at 5.98M, ensuring generative gains reflect regressor capacity rather than expanded latent bandwidth. (iii) High-Resolution STL-10 (24.89M total): A 18.91M parameter U-Net regressor (paired with the 5.98M encoder) fit for 96 × 96 96\times 96 feature maps under fixed memory limits. • Vision Transformers (ViT/DiT): A custom ViT encoder ( E ϕ E_{\phi} , 5.62M parameters; patch size 4 × 4 4\times 4 , embedding dimension 256, depth 6, 8 heads, MLP ratio 4.0, class-token pooling) paired with a continuous diffusion transformer regressor ( DiTContinuous , 58.17M parameters, ≈ 63.8 \approx 63.8 M total) [ 32 , 63 ] . The regressor comprises 12 DiT blocks (patch size 2 × 2 2\times 2 , hidden dimension 384, 6 heads, MLP ratio 4.0). Continuous latents z ∈ ℝ 128 z\in\mathbb{R}^{128} are projected via a 2-layer SiLU MLP and injected additively with timestep embeddings into adaptive layer norm (adaLN-Zero) blocks.

sections.heading: Implementation and Compute Constraints.
sections.text: All models are trained on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU (22.5GB VRAM) using mixed precision ( bfloat16 ). We optimize CNNs with Adam [ 64 ] and vision transformers with AdamW [ 65 ] , both at a base learning rate of η = 2 × 10 − 4 \eta=2\times 10^{-4} . Default hyperparameters are style truncation horizon t 1 = 0.5 t_{1}=0.5 , asymmetric routing cutoff t 0 = 0.05 t_{0}=0.05 , radial Gaussian cutoff r low = 6 r_{\text{low}}=6 (Eq. ( 9 )), and SIGReg weight λ reg = 10 − 3 \lambda_{\text{reg}}=10^{-3} . Under single-GPU resource limits, all benchmarks are evaluated across standard fixed evaluation splits using a single consistent random seed. sections.heading: Flow Regression vs. Single-Step Denoising.
sections.text: Truncated CSFM ( t 1 = 0.5 t_{1}=0.5 ) outperforms both pure autoencoding (58.07%) and unguided linear flow (OT-Flow at 67.11%). Conversely, continuous velocity field regression ( u t u_{t} ) forces the bottleneck to encode persistent content features required to guide transport trajectories through time.

sections.heading: Bridging Generative Reversibility and Discriminative Invariance.
sections.text: Under a budget-constrained training regime of 40K iterations, CSFM achieves 75.29% and 71.94% linear accuracy with 100% and 10% labels, compared to 72.49% and 71.02% for LeJEPA. Conversely, within this computation budget, LeJEPA yields higher performance under 1% labels (67.76%) and neighborhood metrics ( k k -NN: 71.65%, silhouette: 0.1738). This tradeoff reflects distinct geometric organizations: LeJEPA collapses intra-class variance to maximize margins early in training, contracting effective dimensionality ( d 90 % = 9 d_{90\%}=9 ) and creating non-invertible low-density gaps between classes (Figure 1 , right). Standard unguided OT-Flow maintains continuous density across classes but suffers from dispersed, overlapping cluster boundaries ( d 90 % = 31 d_{90\%}=31 ). In contrast, truncated CSFM ( t 1 = 0.5 t_{1}=0.5 ) limits style-subspace variance while retaining ambient coverage ( d 90 % = 37 d_{90\%}=37 ), producing linearly separable semantic clusters alongside a globally connected latent manifold (Figure 1 , middle). sections.heading: Semantic Cardinality: CIFAR-100.
sections.text: Evaluating on CIFAR-100 tests representation robustness under higher label granularity and limited per-class supervision. Standard OT-Flow achieves 42.27% linear accuracy and drops to 10.66% with 1% labeled data (5 samples per class). In contrast, CSFM attains 51.58% linear accuracy ( + 9.31 % +9.31\% ) and 17.65% on 1% labels ( + 6.99 % +6.99\% ). While uniform OT perturbation forces the regressor to resolve high-frequency noise across all scales, CSFM suppresses style variance along the trajectory, preserving linear separability in fine-grained regimes.

sections.heading: Architectural Scalability: Vision Transformers (ViT/DiT).
sections.text: Evaluating transformer backbones demonstrates that CSFM is architecture-agnostic. CSFM scales from 53.30 % 53.30\% at 40K steps to 61.49% at 80K steps ( + 8.19 % +8.19\% ), while standard OT-Flow yields diminishing returns ( 51.84 % → 53.27 % 51.84\%\to 53.27\% ). On 1% few-shot labels, CSFM achieves 49.69%, outperforming OT-Flow by + 8.63 % +8.63\% . Transformers lack local translational inductive biases and typically require aggressive data augmentation; CSFM’s structured trajectories provide a stabilizing generative prior that guides token representations.

sections.heading: Spatial Resolution Scaling: STL-10 ( 96 × 96 96\times 96 ).
sections.text: Benchmarking native 96 × 96 96\times 96 images on STL-10 tests scalability to higher pixel dimensions. Due to GPU memory constraints at this resolution, we employ a lighter, lower-capacity U-Net decoder ( ≈ \approx 19M params) and reduce the batch size from 64 to 16; as established in our CIFAR-10 capacity ablations, reduced decoder capacity inherently lowers representation quality. Nevertheless, pre-training on the 105k uncurated images and evaluating frozen features on the 5k labeled split yields consistent gains over OT-flow: CSFM achieves 65.74% linear accuracy ( + 1.84 % +1.84\% ), 50.54% on 1% labels ( + 2.20 % +2.20\% ), and 57.91% on k k -NN ( + 2.29 % +2.29\% ). This confirms that physical subspace decomposition scales to higher image resolutions without sacrificing content selectivity.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we introduced composite subspace flow matching (CSFM), a generative framework that repurposes continuous normalizing flows for representation learning. By pairing deterministic drift across canonical visual subspaces with a decoupled noise path, CSFM eliminates the irreducible target variance floor of multi-source stochastic diffusion while evaluating in 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}(D\log D) time. We showed that untruncated exponential degradation causes encoders to allocate capacity to high-frequency style details, and proved that a finite style cutoff ( t 1 < 1 t_{1}<1 ) enforces strict feature allocation toward the content subspace 𝒳 c \mathcal{X}_{c} . Empirically, CSFM outperforms unguided flows and pixel-level denoising autoencoders across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10. Under resource-limited training schedules, it proves competitive with discriminative joint-embedding baselines on linear probes while scaling across convolutional and transformer architectures and retaining generative invertibility.

sections.heading: A.1 Simultaneous Diagonalization of Physical Subspace Operators
sections.text: We show that the color, spectral frequency, and illumination operators defined in Section 3.1 mutually commute and admit a common orthonormal eigenbasis. Recall that the observation space factors as ℝ D ≅ ℝ 3 ⊗ ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{D}\cong\mathbb{R}^{3}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{N} ( D = 3 ​ N D=3N ), where ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} denotes the color space and ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{N} ( N = H ​ W N=HW ) corresponds to the spatial component. Because the style operators are orthogonal complements ( P s = I D − P c P_{s}=I_{D}-P_{c} ), an operator commutes with P c P_{c} if and only if it commutes with P s P_{s} , since [ A , I D − P c ] = − [ A , P c ] [A,I_{D}-P_{c}]=-[A,P_{c}] . Thus, establishing commutativity for the content projectors P c P_{c} suffices for all associated style projectors. Proposition 1 . The operators P c color P_{c}^{\rm color} , P c freq P_{c}^{\rm freq} , and P c illum P_{c}^{\rm illum} are mutually commuting symmetric operators: [ P c color , P c freq ] = [ P c color , P c illum ] = [ P c freq , P c illum ] = 𝟎 . [P_{c}^{\rm color},P_{c}^{\rm freq}]=[P_{c}^{\rm color},P_{c}^{\rm illum}]=[P_{c}^{\rm freq},P_{c}^{\rm illum}]=\mathbf{0}. (33) Consequently, they are simultaneously diagonalized by the separable orthonormal basis: Q = U color ⊗ 𝒞 ∈ ℝ D × D , Q=U_{\rm color}\otimes\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}, (34) where U color ∈ ℝ 3 × 3 U_{\rm color}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} is the orthogonal Ohta matrix and 𝒞 = C W ⊗ C H ∈ ℝ N × N \mathcal{C}=C_{W}\otimes C_{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is the 2D orthonormal DCT-II basis. Any linear composition of these operators evaluates in 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}(D\log D) time. Proof. We express each operator over the tensor product space ℝ 3 ⊗ ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{3}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{N} : P c color \displaystyle P_{c}^{\rm color} = Π color ⊗ I N , \displaystyle=\Pi_{\rm color}\otimes I_{N}, where ​ Π color = U color T ​ diag ⁡ ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) ​ U color = u DC ​ u DC T ∈ ℝ 3 × 3 , \displaystyle\text{where }\Pi_{\rm color}=U_{\rm color}^{T}\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0)U_{\rm color}=u_{\rm DC}u_{\rm DC}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, (35) P c freq \displaystyle P_{c}^{\rm freq} = I 3 ⊗ Π freq , \displaystyle=I_{3}\otimes\Pi_{\rm freq}, where ​ Π freq = 𝒞 T ​ Λ freq ​ 𝒞 ∈ ℝ N × N , \displaystyle\text{where }\Pi_{\rm freq}=\mathcal{C}^{T}\Lambda_{\rm freq}\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}, (36) P c illum \displaystyle P_{c}^{\rm illum} = I D − Π color ⊗ Π w , \displaystyle=I_{D}-\Pi_{\rm color}\otimes\Pi_{w}, where ​ Π w = w DC ​ w DC T ∈ ℝ N × N , \displaystyle\text{where }\Pi_{w}=w_{\rm DC}w_{\rm DC}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}, (37) with u DC = 1 3 ​ 𝟏 3 u_{\rm DC}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\mathbf{1}_{3} , w DC = 1 N ​ 𝟏 N w_{\rm DC}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1}_{N} , and Λ freq = diag ⁡ ( { P c freq ​ ( u , v ) } u , v ) \Lambda_{\rm freq}=\operatorname{diag}(\{P_{c}^{\rm freq}(u,v)\}_{u,v}) . The term v DC = u DC ⊗ w DC v_{\rm DC}=u_{\rm DC}\otimes w_{\rm DC} reflects the normalized spatial-color DC vector, so that P s illum = v DC ​ v DC T = Π color ⊗ Π w P_{s}^{\rm illum}=v_{\rm DC}v_{\rm DC}^{T}=\Pi_{\rm color}\otimes\Pi_{w} . Pairwise commutativity follows from the Kronecker mixed-product identity ( A 1 ⊗ B 1 ) ​ ( A 2 ⊗ B 2 ) = ( A 1 ​ A 2 ) ⊗ ( B 1 ​ B 2 ) (A_{1}\otimes B_{1})(A_{2}\otimes B_{2})=(A_{1}A_{2})\otimes(B_{1}B_{2}) . For color and frequency, the operators act on disjoint tensor factors: P c color ​ P c freq = ( Π color ​ I 3 ) ⊗ ( I N ​ Π freq ) = Π color ⊗ Π freq = P c freq ​ P c color . P_{c}^{\rm color}P_{c}^{\rm freq}=(\Pi_{\rm color}I_{3})\otimes(I_{N}\Pi_{\rm freq})=\Pi_{\rm color}\otimes\Pi_{\rm freq}=P_{c}^{\rm freq}P_{c}^{\rm color}. (38) For color and illumination, commutativity reduces to the color factor, where Π color \Pi_{\rm color} is idempotent ( Π color 2 = Π color \Pi_{\rm color}^{2}=\Pi_{\rm color} ): P c color ​ ( I D − P c illum ) = ( Π color 2 ) ⊗ ( I N ​ Π w ) = Π color ⊗ Π w = ( I D − P c illum ) ​ P c color , P_{c}^{\rm color}(I_{D}-P_{c}^{\rm illum})=(\Pi_{\rm color}^{2})\otimes(I_{N}\Pi_{w})=\Pi_{\rm color}\otimes\Pi_{w}=(I_{D}-P_{c}^{\rm illum})P_{c}^{\rm color}, (39) implying [ P c color , P c illum ] = 𝟎 [P_{c}^{\rm color},P_{c}^{\rm illum}]=\mathbf{0} . (43) Evaluating transformations under Q Q requires only channel-wise 2D fast cosine transforms, ensuring that any composition, power, or inverse covariance filtering executes in 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}(D\log D) time. ∎

sections.text: To avoid dimensional collapse, the LeJEPA baseline appends a 3-layer MLP projector to the WideResNet backbone following VICReg [ 15 ] . Current self-supervised paradigms face a trade-off: joint-embedding architectures produce relevant features by aggressively discarding intra-class variance, irreversibly spatial and reconstruction. Conversely, generative models preserve spatial details but struggle to isolate semantics, as their optimization is dominated by pixel variations. To bridge this divide, we propose composite subspace flow matching (CSFM). Rather than corrupting data with unstructured isotropic noise, CSFM formulates representation learning as the variance-minimizing inversion of a deterministic degradation curriculum across spectral, color, and illumination subspaces. By bounding trajectory variance with hard temporal style truncation, a capacity-constrained encoder is driven to ignore transient style artifacts and encode persistent content. Empirical evaluations across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10 show that CSFM yields competitive discriminative transferability while preserving generative synthesis across both convolutional and vision transformer architectures. By avoiding the collapse pathologies of non-generative methods, CSFM forms a smooth latent space that outperforms standard optimal transport flows on linear probing and few-shot classification, while enabling coherent synthesis and trajectory interpolation. These results confirm that steering the physical dynamics of generative flows offers a scalable paradigm for learning representations that are simultaneously linearly separable and generatively invertible. K eywords Representation Learning ⋅ \cdot Flow Matching ⋅ \cdot Generative Modeling ⋅ \cdot Self-Supervised Learning 1 Introduction The primary objective of self-supervised representation learning is to extract informative, high-level, and useful features for downstream tasks from unlabeled raw data [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . While self-supervised learning (SSL) has catalyzed advances across computer vision, natural language processing, and world models for autonomous decision-making [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , extracting representations from unlabelled visual data remains challenging due to the high noise-to-signal ratio inherent to pixel space [ 8 ] . Unlike discrete textual tokens, which represent semantically compressed units, raw pixels are uncompressed physical measurements [ 8 ] . Consequently, high-magnitude nuisance variables, such as localized textures, illumination shifts, and background clutter, statistically dominate the input variance, frequently overshadowing the underlying semantic targets [ 9 , 10 ] . To address these nuisance factors, visual SSL research has largely split into two paradigms with conflicting trade-offs [ 8 ] . On the one hand, reconstruction-based architectures, such as masked autoencoders [ 11 ] and denoising autoencoders [ 12 , 13 ] , model the data distribution by inverting input-space corruptions. However, because standard L 2 L_{2} pixel recovery aligns with raw variance rather than semantic abstraction, these models remain biased toward unpredictable, high-variance details [ 14 , 7 , 10 ] . Conversely, joint-embedding architectures (JEAs), such as VICReg [ 15 ] , and LeJEPA [ 16 ] , circumvent pixel synthesis entirely by enforcing invariance across augmented views in a latent representation space [ 17 , 18 ] . Although this abstraction shields JEAs from nuisance variations, it leaves them vulnerable to informational and dimensional collapse [ 19 , 20 ] . More fundamentally, recent theoretical work reveals a structural friction between discriminative extraction and generative reversibility [ 21 , 8 , 10 ] . To maximize linear separability on semantic tasks, JEAs suppress all intra-class sensitivity. While this invariance maximizes classification margins, it permanently deletes high-frequency and spatial information, rendering the learned representations structurally irreversible and incapable of image synthesis [ 21 , 22 ] . Continuous-time generative models, specifically continuous normalizing flows and diffusion models [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] , provide fully invertible spatial transformations that preserve geometry [ 26 , 24 ] . Recognizing their capacity to model complex distributions without spatial loss, a recent paradigm shift repurposes continuous generative trajectories as proxy objectives for representation learning [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] . By conditioning a continuous vector field on a bottlenecked latent code, the encoder is driven to distill the sufficient statistics required to resolve trajectory ambiguities [ 29 , 30 ] . Because this objective relies on continuous trajectory reconstruction rather than explicit embedding-space invariance, it avoids the dimensional collapse common in JEAs while maintaining spatial reversibility [ 31 ] . Despite this promise, continuous representation models face a significant limitation: standard frameworks rely almost exclusively on isotropic Gaussian noise [ 25 , 23 , 32 ] . This spatially uncorrelated corruption perturbs all image coordinates independently and identically, without accounting for the underlying structure of visual data. Recent generative works have expanded beyond pure Gaussian noise by designing physical degradation trajectories, such as blurring or masking [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] . However, adapting these cumulative multi-operator processes to representation learning proves challenging: sequential noise injections incur an intractable covariance inversion cost and introduce an irreducible target noise floor that disrupts encoder optimization. To resolve these limitations while balancing representation quality with generative reversibility, we propose composite subspace flow matching (CSFM). It replaces uniform corruption with an ordered sequence of deterministic subspace projections spanning the frequency, color, and illumination domains. By pairing this composite drift with a single, decoupled isotropic noise schedule, CSFM yields a simulation-free target vector field that nullifies irreducible target noise with minimal computational overhead. Under this continuous curriculum, content is defined by temporal persistence under physical transport. CSFM isolates content within a capacity-bounded latent code while offloading transient spatial details to the generative vector field, balancing downstream linear separability with a smooth, reversible generative manifold. The core contributions of this work are three-fold: 1. Composite subspace flow matching (CSFM): we introduce a simulation-free flow matching framework that couples an ordered visual degradation path with a decoupled isotropic noise schedule, eliminating target velocity variance with minimal memory overhead 2. Optimal encoder geometry: we show that minimizing trajectory variance induces a block-diagonal precision geometry, prevents features from the style subspace from dominating encoder capacity, and proves that style truncation is necessary for content alignment. 3. Comprehensive empirical validation: across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10 ( 96 × 96 96\times 96 ), using CNN and vision transformer backbones, CSFM outperforms unguided flows and autoencoders in linear and few-shot probing while preserving an invertible, connected latent space for generative decoding. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews self-supervised representation learning paradigms, continuous normalizing flows, trajectory conditioning, and sketched Gaussian regularization. Section 3 introduces CSFM, including the composite projection curriculum, asymmetric gradient routing, and forward-mode analytical computation. Section 4 provides theoretical proofs for subspace disentanglement, capacity saturation, and the style truncation requirement. Section 6 presents our conclusions and outlines directions for future work. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Paradigms of Representation Learning: JEAs vs. Generative Models The goal of self-supervised representation learning is to extract from raw sensory data useful features for downstream tasks, while discarding task-irrelevant style and nuisance [ 36 , 15 , 16 ] . Following recent theoretical formulations [ 22 , 8 ] , an observation x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is decomposed into complementary orthogonal subspaces ℝ D = 𝒳 c ⊕ 𝒳 s \mathbb{R}^{D}=\mathcal{X}_{c}\oplus\mathcal{X}_{s} via x = x c + x s , x=x_{c}+x_{s}, (1) where content x c ∈ 𝒳 c x_{c}\in\mathcal{X}_{c} lies in a low-dimensional subspace ( dim ( 𝒳 c ) = c ≪ D \dim(\mathcal{X}_{c})=c\ll D ) and style x s ∈ 𝒳 s x_{s}\in\mathcal{X}_{s} occupies the orthogonal complement ( 𝒳 s = 𝒳 c ⟂ \mathcal{X}_{s}=\mathcal{X}_{c}^{\perp} ) [ 8 ] . Existing self-supervised methodologies target data decomposition through two diverging paradigms with contrasting trade-offs [ 8 ] . Reconstruction-based generative architectures, such as denoising autoencoders (DAE) [ 12 , 13 ] and masked autoencoders (MAE) [ 11 ] , learn by inverting input corruptions in pixel space [ 8 ] . While this ensures generative reversibility and preserves fine spatial, standard L 2 L_{2} pixel recovery optimizes for total raw variance rather than semantic features [ 14 , 7 ] . Consequently, the encoder exhausts substantial capacity fitting textures and high-variance background noise [ 8 ] . Conversely, JEAs bypass pixel synthesis entirely by training an encoder to match latent representations across independently augmented views [ 37 , 17 , 18 ] . Predicting strictly in latent space protects JEAs from raw pixel [ 8 ] . However, by aggressively discarding all variance orthogonal to the hand-crafted invariances, JEAs permanently discard spatial structure, yielding structurally irreversible representations that are insufficient for image reconstruction [ 21 , 22 ] . Representational Collapse and Latent Regularization. A critical failure mode of optimizing latent invariance in JEAs without generative constraints is representational collapse, wherein representations degrade to a trivial constant vector (information collapse) or span a degenerate lower-dimensional subspace (dimensional collapse) [ 19 , 20 ] . Structured Degradation vs. Decoupled Trajectories. Standard continuous generative models rely on isotropic Gaussian noise, which perturbs all pixel coordinates independently and identically, failing to capture the structured spatial, spectral, and photometric correlations of natural images [ 33 ] .
